title: Living in Australia’s capital: nest site selection by a cavity-dependent endangered parrot
content:
Abstract
Urban habitat management, including the removal of mature trees, may alter the availability of nesting habitat for cavity-nesters in urban landscapes. Effective retention of suitable nesting habitat requires species-specific data on nest-site requirements, which remain poorly quantified. Using climbing surveys, we compared the characteristics of trees and cavities used by the Endangered Gang-gang Cockatoo (Callocephalon fimbriatum) for nesting, with those of non-nesting trees and cavities in urban Canberra, Australia. We also evaluated the proportion of available cavities that meet the requirements for Gang-gang Cockatoo nesting and evaluated the reliability of ground-based cavity counts as a habitat assessment method. We found that Gang-gang Cockatoos used deeper cavities with larger entrance sizes and floor diameters than most available cavities in the study area, and nesting cavities were more likely to be found in trees with more cavities than non-nesting trees. Approximately 20% of unused cavities met the suitability criteria for Gang-gang Cockatoo nesting; ∼80% of those were located in trees already used for nesting. Ground-based cavity counts were not a reliable method for determining the true number of cavities in trees as they consistently under- or overestimated cavity abundance relative to climbing surveys. These findings reinforce that animals can be highly selective in the cavities they choose to nest in and protecting known nesting trees is essential for maintaining breeding habitat for the Gang-gang Cockatoo. Our results also support the need for evidence-based urban habitat management that moves beyond ground-based assessments of habitat quality toward climbing surveys that accurately characterise both cavity availability and suitability.
